title: Multiclass Portfolio Optimization via Variational Quantum Eigensolver with Dicke State Ansatz
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a VQE framework using a parameterized Dicke-state ansatz to encode multiclass portfolio diversification constraints directly in state preparation, removing penalty terms and restricting the search to feasible portfolios. Simulations show that this approach reduces the effective search space and, when paired with the CMA-ES classical optimizer, yields improved convergence, higher approximation ratios, and increased probability of sampling the optimal portfolio; hardware noise remains a challenge and further work on error mitigation and scalability is suggested.
methodology_description: The authors formulate multiclass portfolio optimization as a constrained binary quadratic program (mean-variance objective with per-class equality constraints), convert it to a QUBO and then to an Ising Hamiltonian. Rather than enforcing linear equality constraints via penalty terms, they construct a parameterized variational ansatz that is a tensor product of class-wise Dicke states (fixed Hamming-weight superpositions) so the prepared quantum state lives only in the feasible subspace. They run a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) to minimize the expectation value of the problem Hamiltonian using multiple classical optimizers (CMA-ES, COBYLA, Random Sampler, SPSA, QNSPSA) and compare the Dicke ansatz to other ansatzes (Ry rotations, many TwoLocal variants). Experiments are performed in three problem scenarios with different asset/class/selection configurations; each experiment repeats optimization from many random initial parameter settings, collects measurement samples (shots) from the parameterized circuits, and evaluates performance against a classical optimal baseline (SCIP). Metrics recorded include approximation ratio, frequency of finding the true optimum, sampling probability of the target state, Hamiltonian expectation values, and state fidelities. Some limited runs were also executed on IBM hardware (ibm_pittsburgh) to illustrate noise effects, but the main results are from noiseless simulations (Qiskit Aer GPU).
algorithms_used: Classical optimizers: CMA-ES, COBYLA, Random Sampler, SPSA, QNSPSA
experimental_setup: Simulations run on an Amazon SageMaker instance ml.g5.xlarge (4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA A10G GPU with 24 GB VRAM) under Linux; Python 3.9.5, CUDA 12.4. Qiskit Aer GPU backend used for noiseless circuit simulation. Some additional experiments executed on IBM QPU 'ibm_pittsburgh' to probe noise effects.
dataset_used: Market data downloaded from Yahoo Finance via the yfinance Python library. Two periods listed: 2023-12-18 to 2024-12-16 and 2024-01-02 to 2025-01-02. Asset universes for experiments are constructed from these data (returns, covariance, expected returns).

experiment_input.preprocessing: Compute historical returns, estimate expected returns vector μ and covariance matrix Σ, build mean-variance objective (qx^TΣx − (1−q)x^Tμ + r_f), map binary decision vector x to Ising variables via x_i = (1−z_i)/2. When using Dicke-state ansatz the penalty term for equality constraints is set to zero because feasibility is enforced by the state prep.
experiment_input.notes: All data and tickers are obtainable via Yahoo Finance; authors state datasets are publicly available and downloaded with yfinance.

pipeline_steps: 1) Download historical price data from Yahoo Finance and compute expected returns μ and covariance Σ.
2) Formulate the mean–variance portfolio objective and map the constrained binary problem to QUBO and then to Ising Hamiltonian (xi ↔ zi).

3) Build parameterized quantum circuits: (a) Dicke-state ansatz as tensor product of per-class parameterized Dicke circuits; (b) comparator ansatzes: Ry and multiple TwoLocal variants with matched parameter counts.
4) Initialize ansatz parameters (100 random initial points per experiment; parameters constrained to [0,2π]; seed 42 used for NumPy sampling except for Optuna/CMA-ES cases).
5) For each initialization, run VQE: prepare state, measure Hamiltonian expectation using nshots, and update parameters using a classical optimizer. Repeat for a fixed number of iterations.
6) Repeat experiments (100 runs per optimizer/ansatz configuration) and aggregate results.
7) Compare quantum outputs to classical optimum computed by SCIP and compute evaluation metrics (approximation ratio, probability of ground state, fidelity).
8) Perform limited hardware runs on ibm_pittsburgh to observe noise effects.

key_findings: [supported] A parameterized Dicke-state ansatz can be used within VQE to encode fixed-Hamming-weight (diversification) constraints so that the quantum state initially spans only feasible portfolio configurations, removing the need for penalty terms.

[supported] Using a tensor product of Dicke states reduces the effective search space from 2^n to the product of binomial coefficients ∏_i C(n_i, k_i), concentrating the variational search on the feasible manifold.

[supported] In the reported noiseless simulations across three benchmark scenarios, the parametrized Dicke-state ansatz outperformed Ry and multiple TwoLocal ansatz variants in terms of frequency of finding the global optimum (as the most probable measured state) and in expectation-value error metrics.

[supported] Across the tested classical optimizers, CMA-ES produced the best empirical optimization performance (higher frequency of retrieving the optimum, good convergence behavior and competitive runtime).

[supported] The quality (probability) of sampling the global-optimum bitstring can be improved by increasing the number of classical-optimizer iterations (empirically observed: in Scenario I average p(x*) reached ≥0.95 after ~1500 CMA-ES iterations).

[supported] In simulated experiments with 100 random parameter initializations, CMA-ES frequently concentrated sampling probability on low-energy (high-quality) states and the global optimum more often than other optimizers (COBYLA, SPSA, QNSPSA, Random Sampler).

[supported] Hardware experiments on an IBM QPU using an optimized parameter set that gave 100% probability in simulation produced noisy, degraded distributions: infeasible Hamming-weight states appeared and the global optimum was not the most probable sample — indicating clear sensitivity to current hardware noise.

[supported] The authors provide an empirical formula for the number of parameters in their Dicke-state ansatz: for a class with n qubits and Hamming weight k, np = kn - k(k+1)/2, and for multiple classes np is the sum over classes.

[supported] The authors emphasize they do not claim asymptotic quantum speedup and that potential advantage for variational algorithms is expected only when the number of function evaluations (n_calls = n_shots × n_iterations) is smaller than the effective search space; in their experiments n_calls ≫ n_search_space so no advantage was demonstrated.

[speculative] The paper argues that the Dicke-state ansatz is hardware-agnostic and can be adapted to sparse or 2D connectivity by using alternative Dicke-preparation circuits and parallelization strategies (supported conceptually and referenced to literature, but not demonstrated on constrained topologies).

[speculative] The authors propose that combining the Dicke-state ansatz with CMA-ES and CVaR objective shaping could explore regimes where a practical quantum advantage might appear; this is presented as a direction for future work, not demonstrated.
[supported] Random sampling (baseline) was the worst optimizer in the tested settings.

[speculative] The paper suggests (but does not prove) that restricting the variational manifold to feasible states leads to a smoother optimization landscape and improved sample efficiency compared to general ansatzes — supported by empirical improvement in their experiments but stated as a general explanatory mechanism.
[supported] The VQE-Dicke approach eliminates calibration of penalty multipliers since constraints are enforced by state preparation rather than penalty terms in the Hamiltonian.
results_summary: The study introduces a parametrized Dicke-state ansatz for multiclass portfolio optimization within VQE and demonstrates in noiseless simulations that initializing the variational circuit as a tensor product of Dicke states (one per asset class) confines the search to feasible portfolios, removes penalty terms, and significantly reduces search space. Empirically, across three benchmark scenarios and many runs (100 random initializations × multiple optimizers × 4096 shots), the Dicke ansatz outperformed Ry and multiple TwoLocal variants. CMA-ES gave the best optimization results among tested classical optimizers. Hardware experiments on an IBM device showed substantial degradation due to noise and bit-flip/readout errors, underscoring current NISQ limitations. The authors do not claim asymptotic quantum speedup and note that their experiments do not operate in a regime where a variational quantum advantage can be claimed.
performance_claims: Total experimental scale reported: 100 random initial points × 1000 iterations × 4096 shots per circuit across many ansatz/optimizer combinations; authors state this aggregated to more than ~60 billion executions.
Scenario I (10 qubits, one class, pick 4 -> |D10_4>): search space size 210, Dicke np=30 parameters. SCIP optimal objective -0.818106 (reference).
Scenario II (25 qubits, 5 classes, pick 1 per class -> |D5_1>^⊗5): search space size 3125, Dicke np=20 parameters. SCIP optimal objective -1.474237 (reference).
Scenario III (25 qubits, 5 classes, mixed k values): search space size 25000, Dicke np=31 parameters. SCIP optimal objective -2.00332 (reference).

Table III optimizer counts (Dicke ansatz only, out of 100 runs): Scenario I CMA-ES found the optimal bitstring as most probable in 88 runs (25 runs had p(x*) ≥ 0.95); COBYLA 44/32; QNSPSA 74/65; Random Sampler 27/0; SPSA 49/44. Average times: CMA-ES 82.8 ± 0.6 s, COBYLA 29 ± 4 s, QNSPSA 601 ± 3 s, RS 82.5 ± 0.7 s, SPSA 154.5 ± 0.8 s.
Scenario II (Dicke): CMA-ES 98/97 (All/p>=0.95) average time 181 ± 4 s; COBYLA 49/35 time 43 ± 6 s; QNSPSA 76/73 time 981 ± 9 s; RS 6/0 time 202 ± 1 s; SPSA 40/25 time 302 ± 6 s.
Scenario III (Dicke): CMA-ES 70/1 time 335 ± 12 s; COBYLA 21/5 time 119 ± 21 s; QNSPSA 30/27 time 1541 ± 20 s; RS 0/0 time 376 ± 3 s; SPSA 12/4 time 467 ± 17 s.
Empirical finding: in Scenario I, average p(x*) increases with number of CMA-ES iterations and reached the p(x*) ≥ 0.95 regime for many runs at ≳1500 iterations (Fig. 7).

Hardware QPU (ibm_pittsburgh) test: parameters that give 100% ground-state probability in simulation produced noisy distributions on hardware with infeasible Hamming-weight samples and expectation values far from the ground-state energy (hardware expectation distributions shown far from optimal).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors explicitly state they make no claim of asymptotic quantum speedup. They discuss that potential advantages for variational algorithms might occur when the number of function evaluations is smaller than the effective search space, but their experiments used far more function evaluations than the reduced Dicke search space and are therefore not in a regime demonstrating quantum advantage. Suggestions for future work to explore advantage (e.g., combining Dicke ansatz with CMA-ES and CVaR) are speculative and not demonstrated.
limitations: No claim of asymptotic quantum speedup (author-stated).
Results are primarily from noiseless simulations; only preliminary hardware tests were performed and those showed strong sensitivity to noise and circuit depth (author-stated).
Simulations assume all-to-all qubit connectivity; practical hardware connectivity constraints were not fully incorporated in the main experiments (author-stated).

Experimental regime used (ncalls = nshots × niterations ≈ 4,096,000) is much larger than the effective search space for the tested instances, i.e., ncalls ≫ nsearch_space, so the experiments do not probe the parameter regime where variational quantum algorithms are expected to show advantage (author-stated).

Quality of quantum outputs (probability of measuring the optimal bitstring) is inconsistent and often requires a large number of classical optimizer iterations (e.g., ≳1500 for CMA-ES) to reach high measurement probabilities (author-stated).
Error sources (bit-flip, readout, coherent errors) can break the fixed-Hamming-weight feasibility encoded by the Dicke ansatz leading to infeasible samples on NISQ devices (author-stated).

Error mitigation, advanced transpilation, and circuit-level hardware optimization were not applied in the main experiments; hardware results therefore do not reflect potential gains from these techniques (author-stated).
Scalability to large, real-world portfolio sizes and practical benefits for realistic financial instances are not demonstrated and require further study (author-stated).
The underlying code is not publicly available (author-stated).

[inferred] The approach relies on preparing multiple parameterized Dicke states (one per class) whose combined circuit depth and two-qubit gate count may become large as the number of classes or ki increase, potentially limiting near-term hardware applicability.
[inferred] The Dicke-state advantage depends on ki ≪ ni; when class budgets are not small relative to class sizes, the search-space reduction (and hence benefit) will be diminished.
[inferred] Use of high shot counts (4096) and many optimizer iterations implies large classical evaluation cost; practicality for larger instances or production usage is uncertain.

[inferred] Performance is sensitive to the chosen classical optimizer and its hyperparameters; CMA-ES performed best here but required many function evaluations — the generality of this choice across different instances is unclear.
